source: Veseli, Chibane, Toneva, Koller (2025, COLM) Positional Biases Shift as Inputs Approach Context Window Limits
finding: Lost-in-the-middle depends on how full the window is. It is strongest when input fills up to about 50% of the model's window, peaking near 25% (reasoning) and 38% (retrieval). Past that, primacy weakens, recency stays, and a distance-to-end bias takes over.
numbers: Six instruction-tuned models (Llama-3-70B 8K, Llama-3.1-70B, Llama-3.3-70B, Mistral-Small-24B 32K, Qwen2.5-32B 32K, Gemma-2-27B 8K); relative input lengths 0.06 to 1.0 of window. Reasoning position bias is mostly inherited from retrieval.
quote: successful retrieval is a prerequisite for reasoning in LLMs
limits: Only open models of 70B and below; no frontier closed models; only first/middle/last placement tested, not goal at start AND end.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: put the current subgoal near the END of the prompt (distance bias) and keep input well under the window. Start+end duplication is untested here.

source: Hsieh et al. (2024) Found in the Middle: Calibrating Positional Attention Bias Improves Long Context Utilization
finding: A U-shaped attention bias (high on first and last tokens regardless of relevance) causes lost-in-the-middle. Calibrating out the positional bias improves RAG over standard generation by up to 15 percentage points.
numbers: Up to 15 pp gain over standard generation on RAG; calibrated attention beats prior reordering methods (Table 3).
limits: Needs model internals (attention weights), so not usable through an API. 2024 open models.
agent_relevance: Position effect is an attention property, not a content one. A prompt-only scaffold can only work around it by placement and repetition.

source: Du, Tian et al. (2025) Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval
finding: Even when the model retrieves and recites all evidence perfectly, accuracy still falls 13.9% to 85% as input grows. The drop stays when distractors are replaced by whitespace and even when they are masked out of attention.
numbers: 5 open and closed LLMs; math, QA, coding. Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-v0.3-7B lose large amounts with 30K whitespace (Llama about 59 points off a 96% baseline on one task; Mistral about 44 off 68%). Mitigation 'recite evidence, then solve': GPT-4o up to +4% on RULER; Llama-3.1-8B up to +31.2% on GSM8K.
quote: the sheer length of the input alone can hurt LLM performance, independent of retrieval quality
limits: Mostly 7-8B models plus GPT-4o and Gemini; per-model numbers vary by task.
agent_relevance: Length itself is a cost, not only distraction. Deleting spent context (shorter input) differs from masking it; this supports short contexts. Recite-then-solve is a cheap scaffold step (restate needed state before reasoning).

source: Modarressi et al. (2025, ICML) NoLiMa: Long-Context Evaluation Beyond Literal Matching
finding: With no lexical overlap between question and needle, 11 of 13 models fall below 50% of their short-context baseline at 32K tokens. GPT-4o falls from 99.3% to 69.7%. Reasoning models and CoT also struggle.
numbers: 13 LLMs claiming at least 128K context; short (<1K) vs 32K tokens.
quote: models drop below 50% of their strong short-length baselines
limits: Synthetic needle task; models up to early 2025.
agent_relevance: The effective working set at 32K is far smaller than the advertised window when the link to the goal must be inferred. Supports naming the link explicitly in state.

source: Chroma technical report (2025) Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance
finding: Across 18 frontier models (Claude Opus 4, o3, GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5, Qwen3 and others), performance falls with input length even on simple tasks. One distractor lowers accuracy, four lower it more. Shuffled haystacks beat coherent ones in all 18 models. Focused (~300 token) prompts beat full (~113K) LongMemEval prompts in every family; thinking modes help both but a gap stays.
numbers: 18 models. Refusal rates in the repeated-word task: 2.89% (Opus 4), 2.55% (GPT-4.1), 4.21% (Qwen3-8B). Accuracy values for the main effects are only in charts, not in the text.
limits: Vendor technical report, not peer reviewed; main effect sizes not given in text.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: current frontier models still lose accuracy as context grows, so a focused fresh context per step remains the cheap defence.

source: Lindenbauer et al. (2025, NeurIPS DL4Code workshop) The Complexity Trap: Simple Observation Masking Is as Efficient as LLM Summarization for Agent Context Management
finding: On SWE-bench Verified with SWE-agent, replacing old tool observations with a placeholder (rolling window M=10) about halves cost and matches LLM summarization in solve rate. LLM summaries lengthen trajectories (Gemini 2.5 Flash: 52 turns, +15% vs raw, +13% vs masking).
numbers: Solve rate raw / masking / summary: Qwen3-Coder 480B 53.4 / 54.8 / 53.8; Gemini 2.5 Flash 32.8 / 35.6 / 36.0; Gemini 2.5 Flash thinking 40.4 / 36.4 / 31.4; Qwen3-32B 17.0 / 15.0 / 16.0; Qwen3-32B thinking 23.0 / 24.6 / 24.8. Cost cut 41-57% by masking. Qwen3-Coder with masking: 52% cheaper and +2.6 solve rate.
quote: the most recent context is often sufficient for SE agents
limits: Code agents with verbose tool output (observations about 84% of a turn); M=10 chosen by the authors; error bars about +-4 points; thinking Gemini lost 4 to 9 points under compression.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 8: deleting old observations does as well as summaries at much lower cost, so summaries are not clearly better than pruning. Summaries can prolong runs.

source: Kang et al. (2026, v3) ACON: Optimizing Context Compression for Long-horizon LLM Agents
finding: On AppWorld with gpt-4.1, naive prompt-based history compression loses accuracy (56.0 uncompressed to 43.5); FIFO 45.8, retrieval 27.4, LLMLingua 39.3. Compression guidelines refined from failure analysis (ACON UTCO) recover 56.5 while peak input tokens fall about 26% (9.93K to 7.33K).
numbers: Test-normal, 168 tasks. Observation compression: prompting 42.3, ACON UTCO 53.6. Smaller thresholds cut tokens but lose accuracy; 4096 (history) and 1024 (observation) best. Distilled compressors keep over 95% of teacher performance. Abstract: peak tokens down 26-54%, small models up to +46%.
limits: Guidelines tuned on the same task family; AppWorld, OfficeBench and multi-objective QA only.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: untuned summaries lose needed detail; a rule built from failure cases keeps it. Compression has a sweet spot; more aggressive costs accuracy.

source: Zhou, Qu et al. (2025) MEM1: Learning to Synergize Memory and Reasoning for Efficient Long-Horizon Agents
finding: An RL-trained agent that keeps one compact consolidated state (old turns dropped) beats Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct full-context prompting on 16-objective multi-hop QA: 3.5x performance with 3.7x less memory; peak tokens 27.1% and inference time 29.3% of the 14B baseline.
numbers: Peak tokens nearly constant as objectives grow. MEM1-7B is below the 14B model at few objectives and overtakes it as objectives rise.
limits: Needs RL training; composed multi-objective tasks; not prompt-only.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: a bounded, rewritten state beats a growing history at long horizons, but only after a learned update rule.

source: Wu et al. (2026, v3) ReSum: Unlocking Long-Horizon Search Intelligence via Context Summarization
finding: Periodic summarization of search-agent history, with no training, gives a 4.5% average improvement over ReAct on three benchmarks (including BrowseComp); ReSum-GRPO training adds a further 8.2%.
numbers: Averages: +4.5% (training-free), further +8.2% after RL; a 30B agent trained on 1K samples is competitive with leading open models.
limits: Standard agents are not aligned to read summaries, hence the training gain; averaged over benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: summary-and-continue helps untrained agents only modestly.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation, Section 7.1 (RECAP and SNOWBALL)
finding: Restating all prior information every turn (SNOWBALL) mitigates only 15-20% of the FULL-to-SHARDED deterioration. A final recap turn (RECAP) does better but is unrealistic. Neither restores FULL or CONCAT performance.
numbers: GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini; Code, Database, Math, Actions. CONCAT reaches 95.1% of FULL, so the loss is not caused by rephrasing.
quote: relying on an agent-like framework to process information might be limiting
limits: Restatement was by a simulated user turn, not a code-held ledger; two models only.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: restating the whole problem each step helps only partly. A code-held ledger remains an open test for our scaffold.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Inducing reusable workflows from past successes and giving them to a GPT-4 agent raised WebArena success from 23.5 (BrowserGym) to 35.5 (+12.0 points, +51.1% relative) with about 2.0 fewer steps, and beat human-written workflows (SteP) by 7.6% relative. Mind2Web step success +24.6% relative.
numbers: WebArena 812 tasks; gpt-4-0613, temperature 0; online setting only.
limits: No equal-token comparison: workflows add prompt tokens. GPT-4 2023 model; benchmark specific.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: stored reusable chunks help a lot, but they are not tested against a longer context at equal tokens, so the gap stays open.

source: Sala and Gobet (2017) Experts' memory superiority for domain-specific random material generalizes across fields of expertise: A meta-analysis. Memory and Cognition 45
finding: Experts beat novices on random material in 49 of 55 samples (45 studies, 1,401 participants, p = 9.11e-10). Meta-analysis of 24 studies (28 samples, 903 participants): r = .41 [.29, .51], I2 = 63%; trim-and-fill (8 imputed) r = .29 [.17, .41]. Chase and Simon (1973) is in the binomial table with N = 3 but NOT in the meta-analysis.
numbers: By domain: games .42 (k=11), music .69 (k=5), programming .36 (k=6), sports .30, other .24; domain Q(4)=8.69, p=.069. Exposure time not significant (p=.346). Expertise level not tested as a moderator.
limits: Correction: authors are Sala and Gobet, not 'Gobet et al.'. No chunk counts given. Authors admit working memory as an alternative explanation.
agent_relevance: Settles the b09 inconsistency. The expert advantage on random material fits many small chunks, so the agent cannot assume one big chunk per fact.

source: Thalmann, Souza, Oberauer (2019) How does chunking help working memory? J Exp Psychol Learn Mem Cogn 45(1)
finding: Across four experiments, chunking improved recall of both chunked and unchunked items, so it reduces load rather than only aiding retrieval of the chunk. Benefit held when chunks had unique elements; with overlapping chunks it depended on chunk size. Chunks early in a list helped other material; chunks at the end did not.
numbers: Read from the Europe PMC abstract (PMID 29698045) only; per-experiment effect sizes unavailable (paywalled).
limits: Abstract only. Authors' account: a compact representation is retrieved from long-term memory, which frees capacity.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 (second half) closed at abstract level: chunking frees capacity for other items when the chunk is already in long-term store and comes first. For the agent: put stable named chunks first.

source: Gobet and Clarkson (2004) Chunks in expert memory: evidence for the magical number four ... or is it two? Memory 12(6)
finding: Chess recall and copy tasks (physical board and computer display; game and random positions): most often no more than three chunks were replaced, as template theory predicts. Masters replaced chunks of up to 15 pieces on computer-displayed game positions. Conclusion: chunking theory overestimated STM capacity and underestimated chunk size; Cowan's four may be too high.
numbers: Read from the Europe PMC abstract (PMID 15724362); sample sizes unavailable.
limits: Abstract only; chess only; counts depend on how a chunk is operationalised (pieces replaced between placements).
agent_relevance: Gap 9: justification found at abstract level (few, large, template-based chunks). Suggests a per-step cap of about 2 to 4 items, each a large named structure. Remains a test, not a rule.

source: Hu et al. (2024) HiAgent: Hierarchical Working Memory Management for Solving Long-Horizon Agent Tasks with LLM (abstract page re-check)
finding: Subgoals act as memory chunks; completed subgoals are replaced by summaries, keeping only current-subgoal action-observation pairs. Abstract: roughly double success rate and 3.8 fewer steps on average over five long-horizon tasks. Code linked from the project page.
numbers: No component ablation described in the abstract. Earlier critique: Table 1 overall success 21 to 42.
quote: leverages subgoals as memory chunks to manage the working memory of LLM-based agents hierarchically
limits: Single paper, no independent replication found; d06 and d07 suggest plain deletion captures much of the gain.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: HiAgent stays unreplicated; compare against observation masking at equal tokens.

source: Baddeley and Hitch (1974) Working memory. Psychology of Learning and Motivation 8
finding: Existence and DOI confirmed via Crossref only. Full text not open access this session, so the dual-task numbers could not be extracted.
limits: Paywalled book chapter. Do not cite numbers from it until opened.
